text: . "What year is it?" Regardless of whether you're under house arrest, or under quarantine from a worldwide pandemic, social isolation is not going to be easy. If you're not careful, it can be as deadly as smoking 15 cigarettes a day! So, we've put together some expert advice to help you get through it. After all, we know you have the time to watch this video.

Social isolation may be new to you, but people survive long periods of it all the time. Take astronauts, for example. The longest stretch ever spent in space by one astronaut was 438 days, by Russian astronaut Valery Polyakov. One thing he says helped him survive the isolation was the strict schedule of maintaining the spacecraft. It helped to keep his mind occupied, and his days structured. But you don't have a spacecraft to maintain, so what should you be doing to survive? Luckily for you, we've put together a definitive list of six tips from experts and survivors to answer all your questions.

It might be tempting to fill your lonely days by consuming all the endless online content that's available to you, but staring at a screen all day, every day, can be very bad for you. Not only can it lead to a sedentary lifestyle, it can also cause vision issues, headaches, and chronic neck and back pain. On top of that, the blue light from digital devices suppresses the sleep-promoting hormone melatonin, which could cause trouble sleeping.

Speaking of sleeping, remember to open your curtains and let the sunshine in. This can help you maintain your sleep-wake schedule, which can be disrupted when people are isolated in complete darkness. Messing up this schedule, known as your circadian rhythm, can also lead to depression and fatigue.

You have all the time in the world, so why not get a little creative with it? Write something, paint something, or finish that rock opera you've always dreamed of. Let go of the need to be doing something "important" all the time, and just let your mind wander. It can do wonders for your relaxation, rejuvenation, and personal growth.

If you're isolated for something like a quarantine, you should try to limit the amount of time you spend checking the news. Only check reputable sources, and select one or two times each day when you check them. Checking too often can cause unnecessary stress, and make the time seem to pass more slowly.

Socially isolated doesn't have to mean socially disconnected. In a lot of these situations, you'll still have access to your phone and internet communications. So why not use them? Research shows that those with weaker social relationships are 50% more likely to die over a given period of time than those with stronger relationships. In other words, having social connections is very important for our well-being. Positive social support can help us adjust to challenges and cope with stress. Reaching out to offer support to others is a good way to feel less alone. And it helps you to control your own anxiety by giving you a sense of purpose.

Social isolation may not always feel comfortable. It could make you cry, laugh, yell, and dwell on things that your mind usually wouldn't have time for. But that might not be a bad thing. Let this be an opportunity to push your boundaries of awareness, of time, of yourself, and of your relationships. You may be able to leave this social isolation with a greater appreciation for all the things in your life that you used to take for granted.

So there you have it. Now you know how to make it through this tough time with at least a little bit of your sanity intact. And hey, why not share these tips with your friends? Because above all else, it's important to stay connected with others during a challenge like this. Now that you've survived social isolation, it's time to return to the real world. If everyone else was also living in social isolation that whole time, the real world might look a lot different than you remember. But, whether the economy is in shambles, or the world has run out of toilet paper. We'll have a video to help you survive whatever awaits you.
